questions.question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

To lose one's head

options.text: To lose the track of time

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'Option 2'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom* "To lose one's head" means "To lose one's self-control",* particularly in a situation of pressure or crisis.
 
• **It suggests **a person behaving in a panicked or confused manner, rather than remaining calm and composed.

Therefore, the** correct answer **is: **'To lose one's self control'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Let's explain each option:
 
 
• **"To reach nowhere": **This phrase typically refers to making no progress or getting no results after significant effort. However, this isn't a suitable meaning for "To lose one's head".
 
• **"To have bad memory":** This phrase describes a person who tends to forget things. It doesn't fit the idiom "To lose one's head".
 
• **"To lose the track of time":** This typically describes a situation where a person becomes so engrossed in something that they don't notice how much time has passed. It doesn't align with the meaning of "To lose one's head".

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.**

A bite at the cherry

options.text: An attempt or opportunity to do something
To have a leverage over someone

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'Option 2'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom** "A bite at the cherry"** is used to refer to an opportunity to achieve something or a chance to do something.
 
• **It often refers **to a second chance or another opportunity after missing out on a previous attempt.

Therefore, the **correct answer** is:* 'An attempt or opportunity to do something.'*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Here's why the other options are incorrect:

 
 
• **"A wrong move" -** This phrase means to make an incorrect decision or action, which does not relate to the concept of an opportunity presented in "a bite at the cherry."
 
• **"To have a leverage over someone" -** This phrase means to have a form of power or advantage over another person, which does not correspond with the idea of an opportunity or attempt expressed in the idiom.
 
• **"A dog bite" - **This is a literal translation and does not convey the metaphorical meaning of the idiom "a bite at the cherry," which is about opportunities or attempts, not about physical biting.

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.**

To be in two minds
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** option 1, "In a dilemma". **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The idiom** "to be in two minds"** means **to be uncertain or undecided about something.** It implies that a person is torn between two options or ideas and is unable to make a decision. 
 
• For example, if someone is trying to decide whether to take a job offer in a different city or stay in their current job, they might say "I'm in two minds about it. On one hand, the new job is a great opportunity, but on the other hand, I don't want to leave my friends and family behind." This shows that they are struggling to make a decision and are considering both options. 
 
• Therefore, **option 1, "In a dilemma",** is the best expression of the meaning of the idiom** "to be in two minds".**

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.**

Take your eye off the ball

options.text: To stop paying attention for a moment
Take an advice from a wrong person
Deteriorating and headed for complete disaster

questions.solution:
Here the correct answer is **To stop paying attention for a moment.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The idiom** "take your eye off the ball" **is often used in sports, particularly in games like cricket, baseball, and football, where the ball is the main focus of the game. It means to become distracted or lose focus on the task at hand, especially when it is important. 

 
 
• For example, if a cricket fielder takes his eye off the ball for a moment, he might miss a catch or let the ball go past him, resulting in a run for the opposing team. Similarly, in any other situation, if you take your eye off the ball, you might miss an important detail or make a mistake. 
 
 
 
• Hence, **option 1 - To stop paying attention for a moment **- is the correct answer as it best expresses the meaning of the idiom.
